title: Reciprocal and simple rational functions

points.text: Graph of 1/x and the fact that it is its own inverse

bigPicture: Reciprocal and rational functions have asymptotes, so their graphs split into two branches. Read the asymptotes straight from the equation before sketching.

keyIdeas.answer: Hyperbola in the first and third quadrants with asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0. It is self-inverse: swapping x and y gives the same equation, so the graph is symmetric in y = x.

keyIdeas.cue: Asymptotes and intercepts of y = (ax + b)/(cx + d)?
keyIdeas.answer: Vertical asymptote x = −d/c (denominator zero). Horizontal asymptote y = a/c (the value y approaches as x → ±∞). x-intercept x = −b/a; y-intercept y = b/d.

keyTerms.def: a quotient of two polynomials; here both linear
f⁻¹ = f, so the graph is symmetric in y = x

misconceptions.wrong: Every rational function has horizontal asymptote y = 0
misconceptions.right: For (ax + b)/(cx + d) it is y = a/c.

misconceptions.wrong: The graph can cross the vertical asymptote
misconceptions.right: x = −d/c is not in the domain, so the graph never reaches it.

practice.prompt: f(x) = (3x + 2)/(x − 1), x ≠ 1. (a) Write down the equations of the asymptotes. (b) Find f⁻¹(x).
commonErrors: Algebra slip when collecting x terms

practice.prompt: f(x) = (x + 4)/(2x − 2). State the asymptotes and find the coordinates where the graph meets the line y = x.
commonErrors: Missing the second intersection on the other branch
